title: Train a Tiny Language Model
objective: Build and train a character-level or tiny word-level language model from scratch. Understand the complete training loop end-to-end.
hardware: Any GPU with 4GB+ VRAM, or CPU with 8GB+ RAM
dataset: Any text corpus (Project Gutenberg, Wikipedia dump)
steps: Tokenize your corpus (character or word level)
Build a DataLoader with sequences of length 256
Implement a small transformer decoder
Set up the training loop with cross-entropy loss
Train until loss plateaus
Sample text from the trained model
Evaluate perplexity on held-out text
expectedResults: Loss should decrease consistently. Model should generate coherent short text after training.
troubleshooting: NaN loss: cut LR 10x and check for division by zero. Loss flat: overfit one batch first to verify the loop. OOM: batch 32->8, seq 256->128. Gibberish samples early are normal; worry only if loss never falls.
outcomes: Run an end-to-end training loop you fully understand
Read a loss curve and diagnose basic failure
Sample from your own trained model

title: Train a 10M Parameter Transformer
objective: Train a proper word-piece tokenized transformer with ~10M parameters on a real dataset.
steps: Train or load a SentencePiece tokenizer
Build a tokenized dataset pipeline
Implement transformer with RoPE positional encoding
Train with cosine schedule and warmup
Save checkpoint and sample from model
Compute validation perplexity
expectedResults: Perplexity should reach ~15-25 on natural text. Model generates readable but imperfect text.
troubleshooting: NaN during warmup: extend warmup, verify mask dtype in FP16. Perplexity stuck high: check the data pipeline (decode samples) before blaming the model. OOV explosion: vocab too small for the corpus.
source: Extended nanoGPT approach with proper tokenization
outcomes: Train and use a subword tokenizer
Build RoPE + causal-mask transformer blocks
Run a cosine schedule with warmup

title: Train a 100M Parameter Language Model
objective: Scale up to a 100M parameter model. Learn mixed precision and gradient checkpointing.
architecture: 100M params: ~12 layers, 768 hidden, 12 heads, SwiGLU FFN
steps: Prepare a cleaned dataset of ~1B tokens
Implement transformer with SwiGLU and RMSNorm
Enable BF16 mixed precision
Add gradient checkpointing
Train with proper learning rate schedule
Run evaluation and analyze loss curve
Compare against 10M model performance
expectedResults: Perplexity ~8-12 on natural text. Model should handle longer coherent passages.
troubleshooting: OOM: enable gradient checkpointing, then accumulate; verify the 16 bytes/param + activations budget first. NaN: switch FP16->BF16, confirm warmup ran. Slow: profile dataloader before buying GPUs.
source: Scaling up from 10M with proper engineering practices
outcomes: Train in BF16 mixed precision with AdamW
Use gradient checkpointing deliberately (measure the trade)
Compare two model scales on the same eval

title: Fine-Tune a 1B Parameter Model
objective: Take an existing 1B parameter model and fine-tune it on a domain-specific dataset.
steps: Select a 1B parameter base model
Prepare instruction-tuning dataset
Format data as chat prompts
Run SFT with BF16 full fine-tuning
Evaluate on domain-specific metrics
Compare to base model
expectedResults: Model should follow domain instructions better than base. Watch for catastrophic forgetting of general capabilities.
troubleshooting: Forgetting: cut LR/epochs, mix 5-20% general data. Format leakage: check template consistency train vs serve. OOM on full FT: drop to QLoRA and compare quality.
source: Following standard SFT pipeline with a 1B model
measures: Task win rate vs base (held-out instructions)
Forgetting check: base capabilities spot test
outcomes: Format SFT data with chat templates + response masking
Detect and fix catastrophic forgetting (LR/epochs/replay)
Run a before/after evaluation with baselines

title: QLoRA Fine-Tune a 7B Model
objective: Fine-tune a 7B parameter model using QLoRA on a single consumer GPU.
architecture: 7B model (e.g., Llama 3 8B, Mistral 7B) with QLoRA adapters
steps: Load base model in NF4 quantization
Attach LoRA adapters (rank=16-64)
Format training data with chat template
Run QLoRA training with BF16 mixed precision
Merge adapters and evaluate
Compare QLoRA results to full fine-tuning
expectedResults: Should achieve comparable performance to full fine-tuning at ~60% less GPU memory. Fits on single 24GB GPU.
troubleshooting: Quality gap vs full FT: raise rank to 32-64, target all linear layers, check data quality first. OOM: smaller micro-batch + more accumulation. Bad math/code: verify 8-bit/BF16 before blaming QLoRA.
source: Based on QLoRA paper (Dettmers et al., 2023)
measures: Task quality vs full-FT/LoRA probe (gap on math/code slices)
outcomes: Run NF4 QLoRA end-to-end on one consumer GPU
Choose rank/alpha/targets from measurements
Merge (or serve unmerged) correctly

title: Build an Evaluation Pipeline
objective: Build a reusable eval harness: task set, baselines, regression gates, and contamination screening for your fine-tunes.
hardware: Same GPU you fine-tune on (eval is cheaper than training)
software: Python, lm-evaluation-harness or a small custom runner, your fine-tuned checkpoints
dataset: 200+ held-out task samples mirroring your use case (locked before training)
steps: Collect and lock a held-out task set (PII-scrubbed, dated)
Add baselines: base model, prior checkpoint, trivial heuristic
Fix protocol: shots, decoding (greedy), template, harness version
Screen train-vs-eval overlap (exact + 13-gram + paraphrase probes)
Add a regression gate (metric + threshold) runnable per checkpoint
Report with error bars, not single numbers
outcomes: Size an eval for statistical power
Separate regressions from noise
Gate checkpoint promotion on evals
expectedResults: Every fine-tune gets a scorecard: task delta, general delta, contamination status. Promotion decisions become mechanical.
troubleshooting: Noisy verdicts: add items (n~400 for +/-5%), average seeds/templates. Harness drift: pin versions, re-baseline on change. Judge evals: calibrate vs 50+ human grades first.

title: Quantize and Serve a Model
objective: Take a fine-tuned 7B model to a production-shaped endpoint: quantize, serve with batching, load-test, and observe.
software: vLLM or TGI, Docker, a load generator (simple concurrent client)
dataset: Your eval prompts (p95 mix for load testing)
steps: Quantize the fine-tuned model (INT8 first, then 4-bit; eval each)
Serve behind vLLM/TGI with continuous batching
Verify quality delta on your eval pipeline (gate the deploy)
Load-test with p95 prompt mix; find max concurrency by KV budget
Add health checks, structured logs, and a rollback path
Record cost/token and latency (TTFT/ITL) SLOs
measures: Quality delta per quantization level (task eval)
outcomes: Choose quantization from measurements, not defaults
Size serving from the KV budget
Ship with rollback and observability, not hope
expectedResults: A load-tested endpoint with known cost, latency SLOs, eval-gated deploys, and one-command rollback.
troubleshooting: Quality cliff at 4-bit: check math/code slices, try INT8 or per-group scales. Latency spikes: KV pressure - cap concurrency, chunk prefills. Cold starts: prewarm the engine.

title: Multi-GPU Distributed Training
objective: Scale training across multiple GPUs using data parallelism and FSDP.
steps: Set up distributed environment (NCCL backend)
Wrap model with FSDP
Configure data parallel sampler
Enable gradient checkpointing within FSDP
Run distributed training and profile MFU
Compare throughput to single-GPU baseline
expectedResults: Near-linear speedup with 2 GPUs, diminishing returns with 4+. Target MFU > 40%.
troubleshooting: NCCL errors: NCCL_DEBUG=INFO, pin versions, check fabric. Slow scaling: no_sync on accum steps, NVLink groups for TP. OOM: FSDP FULL_SHARD + CPU offload before adding GPUs.
source: PyTorch FSDP documentation and best practices
outcomes: Launch multi-GPU jobs with torchrun + FSDP
Diagnose comm-bound vs compute-bound scaling
Save/load sharded checkpoints across world sizes

title: Worked Example: 7B QLoRA on a 12GB GPU
objective: INPUT: one RTX 3060 12GB and LLaMA-3-8B (8.03B params). Decide whether QLoRA fine-tuning fits, with numbers reproduced in the toolkit calculators — not vibes.
software: PyTorch, bitsandbytes (NF4), peft (LoRA r=32, alpha=64, all-linear), transformers, BF16 compute
architecture: Frozen NF4 base (8.03B) + 83.9M trainable adapter params (1.04%)
steps: INPUT: record the budget — 12GB VRAM, 8.03B-param base, micro-batch 1 x seq 2048, grad accumulation to effective batch >= 32 sequences.

REASONING: full BF16 fine-tuning costs ~16 bytes/param (2 weight + 4 master + 2 grad + 8 Adam states) = ~128GB for 8B. Impossible here. QLoRA pays 4-bit storage on the frozen base and the 16-byte rate only on ~1% adapter params.
TOOL: VRAM calculator — 8B params, NF4-equivalent base (~0.55 bytes/param with scales = ~4.4GB) + LoRA + BF16 + AdamW + batch 1 x 2048. Read the breakdown, not just the total.
RESULT: base ~4.4GB + adapters/optimizer ~1.3GB + activations ~0.5GB + runtime/CUDA context ~2-4GB = ~9-10GB estimated. Fits 12GB tight; 16/24GB comfortable.
ASSUMPTIONS: check the assumptions list below — NF4 never means exactly 0.5 bytes/param; activation figure is a lower bound (no FlashAttention credit taken).

VALIDATION: run 50 steps, compare torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() against the estimate. If peak exceeds it by >20%, the excess is fragmentation or dataloader workers — profile before shrinking the batch.
NEXT STEP: train 1 epoch, evaluate on a held-out set plus one math/code slice (where 4-bit degradation concentrates), then do the full 7b-qlora project.
assumptions: Frozen base at ~0.55 bytes/param (NF4 + group scales, not raw 0.5)
Adapters 83.9M params (r=32, all-linear) at the full 16 bytes/param mixed-Adam rate
Activations are a lower bound for micro-batch 1 x 2048 without FlashAttention savings
Theoretical estimate: keep ~20% headroom, verify with max_memory_allocated()
expectedResults: Peak allocated memory lands within ~20% of the ~9-10GB estimate on a 12GB card with micro-batch 1-2. Larger deviation means an unmodeled tenant (dataloader RAM, fragmentation, second process on the GPU) — not a wrong method.
troubleshooting: OOM at step 0: base + optimizer don't fit — drop to micro-batch 1, seq 1024, or offload. OOM at step N: leak (retained graph/history), not sizing. Quality gap on math/code: verify 8-bit/BF16 baseline before blaming QLoRA; raise rank to 64 on knowledge-heavy tasks.
source: QLoRA paper accounting (Dettmers et al., 2023); figures reproduced with this toolkit's VRAM calculator
measures: Held-out loss + one math/code slice vs base
outcomes: Size a QLoRA run from first principles
Read a VRAM breakdown instead of trusting totals
Distinguish sizing errors from leaks

title: Worked Example: Sizing a 100M Model From Scratch
objective: INPUT: a from-scratch pretraining idea and one 24GB GPU. Derive a ~100M architecture, its token budget, step count, and memory — all reproducible in the Model and VRAM calculators.
hardware: Single 24GB GPU (fits easily; the point is the method, which scales to 1B+)
software: PyTorch, a BPE tokenizer with 32000 vocabulary
dataset: ~2B tokens (Chinchilla ~20 tokens/param x 100M), cleaned and deduplicated
architecture: 12 layers, hidden 640, 8 heads, non-gated FFN (GPT-2 style, 4x = 2560)
steps: INPUT: fix the budget first — 100M params, ~2B tokens (Chinchilla minimum ~20 tok/param), seq 1024, single GPU.
REASONING: parameters set memory and data needs; tokens/step sets the schedule. Architecture follows from the param target, not taste.

TOOL: Model Calculator — 12 layers, hidden 640, 8 heads, 8 KV heads, vocab 32000, FFN expansion 4.0. The SwiGLU default reads ~120M: that is the 3x-vs-2x FFN difference, so mentally use 2x for this non-gated design = 100.0M. Hidden (640) must stay divisible by heads (8).
RESULT: 100.0M params (embeddings ~41M + attention ~20M + FFN ~39M). Token budget 2B / tokens-per-step (batch x 1024) = step count for the cosine schedule horizon.

TOOL: VRAM calculator — 0.1B params, full BF16 + AdamW, batch 8 x seq 1024: weights 0.2GB + master 0.4 + grads 0.2 + states 0.8 = ~1.6GB before activations. Trivially fits; the same math at 1B says 16GB+ (needs 24GB).
ASSUMPTIONS: see list — Chinchilla 20 tok/param is a minimum for compute-optimality, not a quality guarantee; small models want more.
VALIDATION: overfit one batch to ~0 loss (loop check), then train 1% of steps and confirm the loss curve sits in the expected band before committing to the full run.
NEXT STEP: run the full 100m-llm project with this config.
assumptions: Non-gated FFN: calculator shows the SwiGLU 3x figure (~120M) — the 2x adjustment to 100.0M is exact for this design
Chinchilla ~20 tok/param is a compute-optimal minimum; quality keeps improving past it with good data
Untied embeddings (2 x vocab x hidden); tied would save ~20M here
expectedResults: Model Calculator (with the documented 2x adjustment) agrees with the 100.0M derivation to <1%. VRAM estimate ~2-4GB total — any 8GB+ GPU trains this. Loss on the 1% probe falls fast early (11.7 -> ~4-5) exactly like larger runs.
troubleshooting: Calculator reads ~120M not 100M: you forgot the SwiGLU-vs-non-gated adjustment — the tool assumes gated FFN. Loss flat from step 0: LR ~10x too small or frozen graph, not architecture. NaN at step 0: missing warmup or FP16 without scaling.
source: Chinchilla scaling (Hoffmann et al., 2022) for the token budget; parameter math reproduced with this toolkit's Model Calculator
measures: Tokens/sec to forecast full-run wall time
outcomes: Derive architecture from a parameter target
Convert token budgets to schedules
Know when a result fits one GPU vs needs sharding

title: Worked Example: 100GB Raw Text to Training Dataset
objective: INPUT: 100GB of raw web text. Produce a versioned, tokenized, decontaminated training set with known token count — and know what was thrown away and why.
hardware: CPU machine with 64GB+ RAM for dedup/tokenization; storage ~200GB working space
software: Python, HF tokenizers/datasets, MinHash/LSH dedup, a tokenizer matching the target model
architecture: Not a model project: pipeline is clean -> filter -> dedup -> decontaminate -> tokenize -> chunk/pack -> split -> version
steps: INPUT: 100GB raw text. Estimate yield first: English averages ~4 bytes/token, so ~25B tokens, ~12.2M sequences at seq 2048. Tokenized storage ~50GB as uint16 (vocab < 65536) or ~100GB as uint32.
REASONING: quality beats quantity — a smaller clean set beats a larger dirty one. Every filter stage deletes data for a stated reason; log the retention rate at each stage.
TOOL: Token calculator — confirm the bytes-to-tokens estimate on a 1GB sample with the actual target tokenizer before extrapolating (tokenizer fertility varies 2-3x across languages).

RESULT: staged retention log (e.g., boilerplate removal, perplexity/quality filtering, MinHash near-dedup, eval decontamination), then tokenize -> chunk to seq 2048 -> 99/1 train/val split with the test set locked before training.
ASSUMPTIONS: see list — the 4-bytes/token figure is English-centric; dedup thresholds and contamination windows are choices, not constants.
VALIDATION: detokenize 20 random samples and read them; verify zero n-gram overlap between train and eval above the chosen threshold; confirm the val set was never used for any decision.
NEXT STEP: feed the dataset into wx-100m-scratch sizing, then the 100m-llm training project.
assumptions: ~4 bytes/token holds for clean English; code/multilingual text differs — always measure on a sample
Dedup (MinHash Jaccard ~0.8) and contamination (13-gram overlap) thresholds follow common practice, not law
Packing without document masks leaks context across examples — mask or pad
expectedResults: A versioned dataset (hash + config recorded) with a retention log per stage, ~20-30B tokens depending on filtering aggressiveness, and a provably disjoint eval split. Token estimate from the 1GB sample extrapolates within ~10%.
troubleshooting: Yield far below estimate: boilerplate-heavy crawl (fix extraction) or over-aggressive filters (relax one stage at a time). Eval scores suspiciously high later: contamination leaked — re-check overlap with the benchmark sets. Tokenizer mismatch errors at train time: the dataset was built with a different tokenizer than the model.
source: Standard pretraining data practice (RefinedWeb, Dolma pipelines); quantities reproduced with this toolkit's token calculator
outcomes: Budget a data pipeline by measurement, not hope
Apply dedup and decontamination correctly
Version datasets so runs are reproducible

title: Worked Example: Chasing an Evaluation Regression
objective: INPUT: training loss falls, but your benchmark dashboard drops after a fine-tune. Run the diagnostic protocol that separates real regressions from harness artifacts and noise.
hardware: Same GPU used for training (eval is cheap next to training)
software: Pinned eval harness version, fixed seeds, the pre-fine-tune checkpoint as baseline
dataset: Your held-out eval set (never trained on) + one production-sample slice
architecture: Not a model change: a measurement protocol applied to two checkpoints (before/after)
steps: INPUT: write down the claim precisely — which metric, which split, which decoding, which harness version, both checkpoints. Suppose MMLU-style accuracy reads 62% -> 59% after SFT. Do not act on the headline yet.
REASONING: a score is metric + protocol + noise. Suspects in order: (1) measurement noise, (2) protocol drift (template/shots/harness), (3) contamination shift, (4) real capability loss (forgetting).

TOOL: sizing rule from eval-design — margin of error needs n ~= 16*p*(1-p)/d^2 items; a 3-point move on a 200-item slice is noise, on 2000 items it is signal. Compute the interval before concluding anything.

RESULT: re-run both checkpoints under one pinned protocol (same template, shots, greedy decoding, seeds). If the gap survives, slice it: which subjects/tasks moved? Uniform drops smell like template/format damage; concentrated drops smell like forgetting.
ASSUMPTIONS: see list — greedy, fixed-template evals measure one operating point, not general quality; LLM-judge scores add judge noise.
VALIDATION: confirm train/val overlap is still zero for both runs; confirm the production-sample slice agrees in direction with the benchmark before shipping or reverting.
NEXT STEP: if real — shorten SFT, add general-replay mix, or lower LR; if artifact — pin the protocol in CI so it cannot drift again (the eval-pipeline project).

config.protocol: greedy, fixed template, fixed shots, pinned harness, 2-3 seeds

assumptions: Illustrative 62%-to-59% move is hypothetical method demonstration, not a measured result
Benchmark scores are not universal quality — they answer 'did this benchmark move', not 'did the model improve'
Contamination cuts both ways: a drop can mean the new run is honestly cleaner
expectedResults: A verdict in one of three bins — noise (intervals overlap), artifact (gap vanishes under pinned protocol), or real regression (survives pinning, visible in slices) — each with a prescribed next action. No verdict without the interval calculation.
troubleshooting: Gap vanishes on re-run: protocol drift was the bug — diff harness versions, templates, and chat markers. Everything flat including baseline: harness broken, not the model. Production slice disagrees with benchmark: trust production, the benchmark is off-distribution.
source: Eval-design sizing and protocol guidance from this toolkit's evaluation curriculum
outcomes: Never ship or revert on a headline number
Separate noise, artifact, and real regression
Pin eval protocols in CI

title: Worked Example: 8B Inference From 6 to 32 Concurrent Users
objective: INPUT: LLaMA-3-8B on one 24GB card, users complain about latency at 6 concurrent chats with 8k context. Engineer the memory budget to 32 concurrent without new hardware.
hardware: Single 24GB GPU (RTX 4090-class); vLLM-style server with paged KV management
software: Continuous-batching inference server, FP8/INT8 KV support, 4-bit weight option, prefix caching
dataset: Production chat sample: measure real prompt/completion length distribution first
architecture: LLaMA-3-8B: 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128 (131 KB/token BF16)
steps: INPUT: baseline budget — weights BF16 16GB + KV per request (2 x 8192 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2B) ~= 1.07GB x 6 = 6.4GB + runtime ~1.5GB ~= 24GB. Saturated: the 7th concurrent request OOMs or queues.
REASONING: weights are fixed cost; KV is per-request cost. Concurrency = (VRAM - weights - runtime) / KV-per-request. Shrink either term deliberately, measuring quality at each step.
TOOL: Inference Memory calculator — enter 8B, 32 layers, hidden 4096, 32 heads, 8 KV heads, batch 6, context 8192. Confirm ~24GB, then change one knob at a time.

RESULT: cap effective context to 4k for this workload (halves KV to ~0.54GB/req), switch KV cache to FP8/INT8 (~0.27-0.54GB/req — verify quality on evals), quantize weights to 4-bit (~4.4GB), enable prefix caching for the shared system prompt. New budget: 4.4 + 32 x ~0.5 + runtime ~= ~22GB for 32 concurrent.
ASSUMPTIONS: see list — KV quantization and context caps trade quality/capability for capacity; the production length distribution decides whether the cap is safe.

VALIDATION: load-test at 32 concurrent with real prompt shapes; watch p99 latency (queueing explodes past ~70% sustained utilization without admission control) and KV-hit rate; re-run quality evals on the quantized + capped configuration.
NEXT STEP: productionize with concurrency caps, observability (KV pressure, queue depth, TTFT/TPOT), and the full serve-quantized project.

config.optimized: 4-bit weights ~4.4GB + FP8/INT8 KV ~0.5GB/req x 32 + prefix caching

assumptions: Per-request KV figures are theoretical (paged allocation fragments less than naive contiguous math)
8-bit KV is frequently near-free on quality but must be verified per workload — 4-bit KV needs evals
Context caps are safe only if the measured production distribution fits; long-tail users need a separate tier
Decode is bandwidth-bound: batching multiplies throughput until KV traffic competes
expectedResults: Calculator-predicted ~22GB at 32 concurrent; load test confirms p50 latency near single-request levels with bounded p99 under admission control. Quality evals on the final (quantized + capped) config show no regression beyond the pre-agreed threshold.
troubleshooting: Still OOMing: fragmentation from a non-paged allocator (looks like a leak — switch to paged), or one giant prompt blowing the cap (enforce max length server-side). p99 explosion: utilization too high — cap concurrency, add replicas. Quality drop on math/code: KV/weight quantization bites there first — test 8-bit before 4-bit.
source: KV-cache formula and batching guidance from this toolkit's inference curriculum; figures reproduced with the Inference Memory calculator
measures: Calculator prediction vs nvidia-smi at 32 concurrent
Quality evals on the exact serving config (weights + KV + cap)
outcomes: Budget inference as weights + KV x concurrency
Apply KV quantization and context caps deliberately
Load-test with admission control before declaring victory
